title.rendered: Earhart expedition update: Crew arrives onshore, sets up operations on Nikumaroro

content.rendered:
NIKUMARORO, Kiribati — Members of the Taraia Object expedition, a joint effort between the Archaeological Legacy Institute, Purdue Research Foundation and Purdue University, made it ashore Nikumaroro on Tuesday (Oct. 13), where they began setting up equipment and operations for their investigation into an anomaly that could be what remains of Amelia Earhart’s Lockheed Electra 10-E.

Through the Amelia Earhart Fund for Aeronautical Research, the Purdue Research Foundation funded Earhart’s Lockheed Electra “Flying Laboratory.” Earhart intended for the plane to be returned to Purdue upon completion of her round-the-world flight.

It was the first day onshore for the 17-person expedition team, who arrived too late Monday (Oct. 12) to visit the island after five days of sea travel. As the sun rose, some crew members took smaller transport boats from the Marin Mainiku into the lagoon. The remaining team members set up staging areas and cleared a path to support fieldwork that will begin Wednesday (Oct. 14).

Onshore Earhart work begins

The sun rises over Nikumaroro.

Onshore Earhart work begins

Boilermakers Steve Schultz (left) and Sirisha Bandla gear up for the ride to the island.

Onshore Earhart work begins

Life vests dry on a palm tree.

Onshore Earhart work begins

The team uses smaller transport boats to navigate to the island.

Onshore Earhart work begins

Canopy tents provide staging areas for the team.

Onshore Earhart work begins

The shore of Nikumaroro’s lagoon.

Onshore Earhart work begins

Expedition team members return to the Marin Mainiku each evening after working on the island.

After many years since the last expedition to the island, the traditional path to the lagoon, nicknamed the “Gallagher Highway,” was heavy with undergrowth and coconuts underfoot. Supported by crew members from the Marin Mainiku, the team used a combination of machetes and hand chain saws and finished cutting a trail to the lagoon within two hours. At least four coconut crabs were encountered along the way, but they posed no threat to the operation.

Though the team expected to spend an entire day setting up operations, the work was accomplished by lunchtime. The joint team, composed of expedition members and the vessel crew, was able to access the Taraia Peninsula by 1 p.m. local time. Nikumaroro is 17 hours ahead of Eastern time in the U.S.

At the peninsula, the team walked the sandspit to look for artifacts in the first phase of terrestrial archaeology work. A series of canopy shelters was erected and sandbags were filled. The first components of the tech system were erected, and the maritime archaeology team assessed the conditions of the research site, including the sediment on the lagoon floor.

Operations were wrapped up by 4 p.m., and the expedition team retraced its steps to the south side of the lagoon and back through the Gallagher Highway to the beach at the head of the “blasted channel,” a man-made opening near the southwestern corner of the island’s perimeter reef. There, they were picked up by the vessel’s transport boat and carried through large swells back to the Marin Mainiku, where they retired for the evening.

title.rendered: Earhart expedition update: Crew arrives at Nikumaroro, launches critical phase of Amelia Earhart plane search

content.rendered:
NIKUMARORO, Kiribati — Following a five-day, 830-nautical-mile voyage across the remote South Pacific, the 17-person Taraia Object expedition team, supported by a 17-person boat crew, arrived Monday (Oct. 12) at Nikumaroro to start its investigation of a visual anomaly spotted in satellite imagery that may be what remains of Amelia Earhart’s Lockheed Electra 10-E.

The Marin Mainiku arrived at approximately 8 p.m. local time on the western side of the uninhabited atoll, part of the Phoenix Islands of the Republic of Kiribati. Nikumaroro is 17 hours ahead of Eastern time in the United States.

“It is incredibly rewarding to be this close to completing our inspection of the Taraia Object and potentially solving, at long last, the outstanding mystery of the disappearance of Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan more than 89 years ago,” said Rick Pettigrew, executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and leader of the expedition.

The expedition is the result of years of research on the Taraia Object hypothesis by Pettigrew and ALI, which builds on the castaway hypothesis established and documented by The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery over the past nearly 40 years. Pettigrew approached Purdue University and the Purdue Research Foundation in February 2025 due to the university’s historic connection to Earhart. Through the Amelia Earhart Fund for Aeronautical Research, the Purdue Research Foundation funded Earhart’s Lockheed Electra “Flying Laboratory.”

Since the expedition team arrived after sunset, no field operations took place immediately. Instead, the Marin Mainiku proceeded to the island’s eastern end for calmer overnight sea conditions, and the team spent the evening making final preparations to go ashore at daybreak through the “blasted channel,” a man-made opening near the southwestern corner of the atoll’s wide and imposing perimeter reef.

Pettigrew said it has been seven years since the last authorized expedition set foot on Nikumaroro and more than 15 years since anyone has been on the Taraia Peninsula. While there, the team will also conduct biological and environmental surveys of the area in coordination with the Kiribati representatives on the expedition.

The first day on-site will focus on transporting equipment, clearing vegetation, and establishing staging operations at the beach and on the south side of the lagoon. Upon reaching shore, the team will divide into two teams, with one taking smaller transport boats through the Tatiman Passage, a natural opening on the island’s western side, to access the lagoon and place buoys along the way to guide a return trip to the Marin Mainiku at the conclusion of work.

The second team will begin marking and cutting a trail through the jungle from the landing site at the beach to a designated spot on the south side of the island’s lagoon, where it will rendezvous with the boat team. Staging areas will be established on both ends of the jungle trail to support the first day’s work, before the focus moves to the Taraia Peninsula on Wednesday (Oct. 14).

Earhart team underway

The expedition team enjoys breakfast on the Marin Mainiku.

Earhart team underway

From left: Boilermakers Sirisha Bandla, Steve Schultz and Marc Hagle eagerly anticipate reaching Nikumaroro.

Earhart team underway

Expedition team lead Rick Pettigrew, left, poses with Steve Schultz, Purdue general counsel, at the rail.

Earhart team underway

Represented by a blue dot, the Marin Mainiku approaches Nikumaroro.

Earhart team underway

Aaron Arrants, medic and safety officer, points to the navigation system to show the ship has arrived at Nikumaroro.

Once at the peninsula, the first piece of investigative work will be a survey of the sand spit at the tip to identify the presence of any surface artifacts before beginning maritime archaeology work. The maritime specialists will first deploy a surface boat to lay out a series of parallel transect lines — a process to establish a systematic grid for conducting the search for artifacts, then measuring and recording them. The team will then use a magnetometer to detect the presence of ferrous metals. Although the Electra was largely made of aluminum, steel cabling and other metal components of the aircraft could give a ferrous metal reading.

In the next phase, various sonar technologies will be used to detect objects under sediment along the lagoon floor, and the archaeology team will use a hydroprobe to contact the object directly to determine its depth, orientation and surface composition. Finally, a water induction dredge will be used to remove sediment for visual inspection of the object. Based on estimates from aerial photos, the Taraia Object is believed to be located only 10 feet from the lagoon’s shore, and depending on the tide, under as little as 5 feet of water, plus a layer of sediment of unknown depth.

Although the crew has successfully reached Nikumaroro, prevailing weather and sea conditions will continue to be a factor in conducting operations. The effects of El Niño remain present around the island, and daily access to shore will depend on tides and safe boating conditions. The crew will sleep nightly aboard the Marin Mainiku for a number of reasons, one of which is the presence of coconut crabs, whose size and overnight activity make staying on the island impractical. The team is expecting to spend five days on the island to complete its fieldwork before beginning the return to Tarawa.

“Despite the inevitable challenges of carrying off an endeavor of this magnitude, and the difficulties of sailing across the vast Pacific in a working vessel to reach a place as remote as this one, our team is in excellent spirits,” Pettigrew said. “We continue to be well taken care of by our very capable Kiribati crew, and we are looking forward to the work ahead.”

title.rendered: Earhart expedition update: Crew at sea, expected to arrive on Nikumaroro in 72 hours

content.rendered:
HALFWAY BETWEEN TARAWA AND NIKUMARORO, Kiribati — The Marin Mainiku, the Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel transporting the Taraia Object expedition team, is approaching the halfway point Friday as the crew continues its voyage across the vast South Pacific toward Nikumaroro Island.

The Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI), Purdue Research Foundation and Purdue University have embarked on this expedition in an attempt to solve the disappearance of Amelia Earhart during her mission to become the first person to fly around the world at the equator. Their focus will be inspecting the Taraia Object, an anomaly in Nikumaroro’s lagoon first noticed in satellite imagery in 2020 and later confirmed to be visible on aerial photos taken as far back as 1938.

The vessel is making good time and is tentatively expected to arrive at Nikumaroro around midday Monday, Oct. 12, local time.

Traveling at an average speed of 7 knots, or about 8 miles per hour, the crew had sailed approximately 370 of the 830 nautical miles from Tarawa, Kiribati, to Nikumaroro at the time of this publication.

Earhart team underway

From left: Boilermakers Steve Schultz, Sirisha Bandla and Marc Hagle enjoy the view from outside the pilothouse.

Earhart team underway

The crew reports mostly calm seas and favorable wind conditions.

Earhart team underway

Steve Schultz, left, poses with Helmut Schleppi, filmmaker.

Earhart team underway

Expedition team members test equipment ahead of their island arrival.

Earhart team underway

Technology specialists Sirisha Bandla, left, and Laura Kennedy, right, pose with Steve Schultz.

Earhart team underway

Sunrise over the Pacific Ocean.

Located about 1,800 nautical miles south of Hawaii and more than 230 miles from the nearest inhabited island, Nikumaroro is among the most isolated places on Earth. The coral atoll has long been central to theories surrounding Earhart’s disappearance in 1937.

The crew reports mostly calm seas and favorable wind conditions as they continue on their journey. No other ships are nearby, but despite the remoteness, they are amazed they are able to stay connected and communicate with satellite technology. They have also reeled in two fresh tuna to add to their regularly scheduled meals at sea.

“We saw photos and had a pretty good idea of what we were getting into, but nothing can prepare you for the real thing,” said Steve Schultz, Purdue senior vice president and general counsel, serving as Purdue’s expedition team lead. “The sights, the sounds and overall conditions on a working ship plying through the rolling ocean swells is a unique experience. But we all signed up for a seafaring adventure, and we’re focused on the work ahead.”

Three members of the team have visited Nikumaroro before, including expedition leader Rick Pettigrew, ALI executive director; Aaron Arrants, safety officer for the expedition; and Renato LaRocca, ALI field assistant and retired cancer medicine physician.

“Having had the honor of being on many tropical islands around the world, Nikumaroro is up there from an aesthetic point of view,” LaRocca said. “Of course, things that are equally important: absent mosquitoes, no snakes, no spiders. Now, there is a problem with coconut crabs and hermit crabs, but otherwise it’s a magical place.”

Once the vessel reaches Nikumaroro, the crew will use a drone to survey the island before beginning the complex process of positioning specialized equipment for use at the Taraia Peninsula. That includes getting equipment off the vessel and onto a smaller transport boat, then navigating the “blasted channel” through the island’s high reef to reach the beach.

On the island, the team will divide into two groups, with one assigned the task of cutting a passage through the jungle to the island’s lagoon, while the other guides additional smaller boats around the island’s southern perimeter to reach the natural opening of the lagoon, known as the Tatiman Passage, on its western end. The team will then reunite on the south side of the lagoon, where they will establish a staging area. That will be the jumping-off point each day for the work at the Taraia Peninsula on the north side of the lagoon.

“We will start our remote sensing work using magnetometers and sonar to get a better idea of what is there before we actually uncover it. After that is all done, we will uncover it using a hydraulic dredge,” Pettigrew said.

The expedition is the result of years of research into Earhart’s disappearance by Pettigrew, the Archaeological Legacy Institute and members of The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery. After reviewing evidence collected, Pettigrew approached Purdue and the Purdue Research Foundation in February 2025 due to the university’s historic connection to Earhart. Through the Amelia Earhart Fund for Aeronautical Research, the Purdue Research Foundation funded Earhart’s Lockheed Electra “Flying Laboratory.”

title.rendered: Earhart expedition update: Crew begins 6-day sea voyage to South Pacific atoll Nikumaroro

content.rendered:
TARAWA, Kiribati — The Taraia Object expedition team began the next leg of its journey — and its first seaborne one — departing Tarawa, Kiribati, on Wednesday aboard a Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel en route to Nikumaroro, the remote Pacific atoll where the team will search for evidence of Amelia Earhart’s missing Lockheed Electra 10-E.

The 17-person expedition team includes representatives from the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI), Purdue Research Foundation, Purdue University, RECON Offshore and the Republic of Kiribati. The Purdue Research Foundation originally funded the Lockheed Electra “Flying Laboratory” through the Amelia Earhart Fund for Aeronautical Research as part of Purdue’s pioneering efforts in aviation.

Earhart was attempting to become the first person to circumnavigate the globe at the equator. She had completed 22,000 miles of a 29,000-mile route in July 1937 when she and her navigator, Fred Noonan, vanished en route to Howland Island, about 400 miles north of Nikumaroro.

Following the loading of equipment and a safety briefing, the expedition team and 17-person boat crew departed Tarawa aboard the Marin Mainiku at about 7:30 p.m. local time Wednesday. Tarawa is 16 hours ahead of Eastern time in the United States.

Over the next six days, the Marin Mainiku will travel approximately 830 nautical miles at an average speed of 8 knots, or about 9 miles per hour, before reaching Nikumaroro around Monday, Oct. 12.

Early reports from the expedition team indicate the vessel encountered heavy seas upon leaving Tarawa’s large lagoon. The prevailing sea state and tide effects of El Niño are anticipated to be a key consideration during the voyage, including upon arrival at Nikumaroro. That is when the Marin Mainiku’s landing craft will need to navigate a narrow passage known as the “blasted channel,” a gap in the island’s high reef created by the British government during its evacuation of colonists in 1963 — the last time the island had inhabitants.

On board the Marin Mainiku, the team had its first meal of chicken stew. Each crew member has a designated sleeping pod equipped with a mattress and pillow, along with space for personal belongings.

Earhart team departs

The expedition team includes three Boilermakers (from front left): Marc Hagle, Steve Schultz and Sirisha Bandla.

Earhart team departs

Expedition team members Steve Schultz and Rick Pettigrew pose for a selfie.

Earhart team departs

Equipment was shipped from multiple points in the United States and loaded onto the boat in Tarawa.

Earhart team departs

The expedition team enjoys a sunset departure from Tarawa.

Earhart team departs

Each crew member has a designated sleeping pod equipped with a mattress and pillow.

Earhart team departs

The team enjoys its first breakfast on the Marin Mainiku.

“It doesn’t have all the creature comforts we’re accustomed to, but the Marin Mainiku has everything we need,” said Steve Schultz, the university’s senior vice president and general counsel who serves as the Purdue team lead for the expedition. “This isn’t a pleasure cruise. But it’s our home for the next three weeks, and we’re happy to be aboard and underway. The members of the ship’s crew are seasoned professionals, and we’re in good hands for this passage.”

The expedition team’s top priority during its first full day at sea will be to inventory and test the equipment shipped from multiple points in the U.S. — including Eugene, Oregon, and Pensacola, Florida. Since the team will be wholly self-sufficient on the island, the group needs to ensure they have the power necessary to conduct planned work, making a workable solar array and solar power station a mission-critical concern. Detection tools they will be using include a side-scan sonar, a magnetometer and a hydraulic dredge, together with a range of other equipment designed not only to identify the Taraia Object, but also to gather tidal and environmental baseline data for Kiribati.

“We might as well be going to the moon,” said Sirisha Bandla, one of the expedition’s technology specialists and member of Purdue’s Cradle of Astronauts. “Having left Betio Port, we’re now on our own, but grateful to be in the hands of the ship’s capable crew, at least for now. When we get to Nikumaroro, though, we’re going to need to rely on the equipment we designed and deployed for this purpose. I’m looking forward to moving it from storage to working mode and confirming that it all works. I’m confident it will, but if we need to make adjustments, well, that’s exactly what Boilermakers are for.”

title.rendered: Earhart expedition update: Crew arrives at Tarawa, prepares for departure

content.rendered:
TARAWA, Kiribati — Fourteen members of the Taraia Object expedition — the Archaeological Legacy Institute, Purdue Research Foundation and Purdue University’s joint expedition to explore a Pacific island lagoon for Amelia Earhart’s missing plane wreckage — arrived Tuesday (Oct. 6) at Tarawa, Kiribati, the expedition’s staging area. After linking up with the expedition’s three Kiribati representatives on Tarawa, the team is now complete and ready to begin the sea voyage to Nikumaroro, a remote atoll halfway between Australia and Hawaii.

The team arrived at approximately 10 a.m. local time following a flight from Nadi, Fiji, where they had spent a day on briefings and training activities. Tarawa is 16 hours ahead of Eastern time in the United States. Team members spent their first day in Tarawa managing logistics, checking equipment and meeting with officials of the Kiribati National Shipping Line ahead of their planned departure at 3 p.m. local time on Wednesday (Oct. 7).

Earhart team departs

Members of the Taraia Object expedition team at the airport en route to Tarawa.

Earhart team departs

Expedition team members Rick Pettigrew and Marc Hagle point out Nikumaroro on a large map.

Earhart team departs

Steve Schultz (left) poses for a picture with fellow expedition team members Ren LaRocca and William Wilson.

“Even today, given its sheer vastness, there’s something significant to flying over the Pacific Ocean,” said Sirisha Bandla, expedition member, Purdue alumna and member of the Cradle of Astronauts. “As we finally arrived at our point of departure here in Tarawa, it struck home that we’d flown over a majority of the portion that Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan were attempting to traverse when they were lost. Now we hope to have a chance to bring closure to their story.”

“Moving a team of this size — and with this much equipment — halfway around the world is a huge logistical feat,” said Steve Schultz, Purdue’s senior vice president and general counsel. “Even when you think you’ve done enough planning and preparation, everything has to fall into place once you’re underway. The amazing thing is that it has been a series of small victories. Customs, logistics and other details we’ve sweated over for months now all came together in rapid succession over the past three days.” 

Next, the crew will depart Tarawa, by sea, for the longest leg of their journey to Nikumaroro in the Phoenix Islands of Kiribati. The team will sail six days and is expected to arrive at Nikumaroro on Oct. 13 and then spend the following days on the small island in the search effort.

title.rendered: 1 week out: Countdown to the search for Amelia Earhart’s plane begins

content.rendered:
WEST LAFAYETTE, Ind. — In one week, the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI), Purdue Research Foundation (PRF) and Purdue University will embark on an expedition to the South Pacific in an attempt to solve the disappearance of Amelia Earhart during her mission to become the first person to fly around the world at the equator.

The expedition will include almost three weeks of travel and research to determine if a visual anomaly spotted in satellite images of Nikumaroro’s lagoon is Earhart’s missing Lockheed Electra 10-E. The search originally was announced in July 2025, 88 years to the day that Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan mysteriously disappeared.

Richard Pettigrew, executive director of ALI, is leading the expedition team traveling to Nikumaroro. With the journey’s launch approaching quickly, he said the prospect of setting off on a discovery mission of this potential magnitude is exhilarating.

“With just a week to go before the launch of our expedition, my conscious focus is on the execution of our fieldwork plan,” he said. “Inevitably, though, this comes with an array of strong feelings. I’m intensely and eternally grateful to the many individuals and organizations who have helped to make our vision real. I feel truly lucky to be in a position to possibly solve one of the greatest mysteries of all time, whether or not that happens.”

The expedition was delayed in October 2025 as the team worked through additional stages of the permit approval process with the Republic of Kiribati, the island nation in which Nikumaroro is located. The onset of the South Pacific cyclone season during the winter months prevented a safe departure later in 2025.

Expedition members will rendezvous at Tarawa, Kiribati, on Oct. 6 and depart by sea the next day for Nikumaroro in the Phoenix Islands of Kiribati. The team will sail six days to arrive at Nikumaroro and then spend the following days on the small island in the search effort.

Three Purdue representatives will be part of the crew: Steve Schultz, senior vice president and general counsel, and Sirisha Bandla and Marc Hagle, both alumni and members of Purdue’s Cradle of Astronauts.

Work on Nikumaroro will focus on inspecting the Taraia Object, first noticed in satellite imagery in 2020 and later confirmed to be visible on aerial photos taken of the island’s lagoon as far back as 1938.

Initial work will include videos and still images of the site prior to any disturbance, followed by remote sensing with magnetometers and sonar. Then the team will employ underwater excavation using a hydraulic dredge to expose the object for identification. Fieldwork will include a walk-over survey of nearby land surfaces to search for debris washed up by waves.

The expedition is scheduled to arrive back in Tarawa around Oct. 22 and fly home the following day.

For Pettigrew, the mission offers the opportunity to solve one of the greatest mysteries of the 20th century.

“Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” he said. “Other evidence already collected by The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery establishes an extremely persuasive, multifaceted case that the final destination for Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan was on Nikumaroro. Confirming the plane wreckage there would be the smoking-gun proof.”

The Purdue Research Foundation originally funded the Lockheed Electra “Flying Laboratory” through the Amelia Earhart Fund for Aeronautical Research as part of Purdue’s pioneering efforts in aviation.

“Amelia’s legacy remains strong at Purdue, and she looms large in our canon of heroes,” Schultz said. “Successfully identifying the Electra would be the first step toward fulfilling her intention to return it to the university. Additional work and further conversations with Kiribati would still be needed to make that a reality, but we feel we owe it to her legacy at Purdue to try to find a way to bring it home if we find it.”

Any effort to extract and return the aircraft wreckage to West Lafayette would require permission of the government of Kiribati, Schultz said. ALI and Purdue credit the country’s leadership and support with making the expedition happen.

“For Kiribati, Nikumaroro is much more than the possible setting for one of the world’s great historical mysteries,” said the Honorable Minister Mikarite Temari, head of Kiribati’s Ministry of Line and Phoenix Islands Development. “It is part of our heritage, and we have a responsibility to protect and better understand it. We are pleased to partner with Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University in this effort to learn more about the Taraia Object and to share the story of Nikumaroro and Kiribati with the world. We also see this expedition as an opportunity to build a lasting partnership that can help support important priorities such as regenerative tourism, cultural preservation, education, advances in aviation technology and economic development for our people.”

Earhart began her attempt to circumnavigate the globe and set a record for long-distance flight in late May 1937, flying out of Oakland, California.

“This Is Purdue,” the university’s official podcast, released a four-part miniseries called “Finding Amelia” on Monday (Sept. 28). The storytelling centers around the decades-long connection between the legendary aviator and Purdue. The miniseries is available to listen to on the podcast’s website or wherever you get your podcasts, and each episode is available to watch on YouTube.

The miniseries digs into who Amelia was and her journey to the university, the “Flying Laboratory” she was operating when she disappeared, the Amelia Earhart Collection within Purdue University Archives and Special Collections, and the upcoming Taraia Object expedition.

Earhart, already an aviation legend in the 1930s, came to Purdue in 1935 and worked for two years as a women’s career counselor and advisor in the university’s aeronautics department. The recently opened Amelia Earhart Terminal at the Purdue Airport honors her legacy as a valued Boilermaker. She is also remembered across campus through facilities, programs and clubs.

Bandla, a 2011 Purdue graduate in aeronautical and astronautical engineering, said she remembers the campus memorializing Earhart in so many ways.

“Purdue’s legacy is built on turning ambitious ideas into meaningful impact, and that is something that has always made me proud to be a Boilermaker,” Bandla said. “To be part of this expedition is both exciting and deeply meaningful. We are searching for answers behind one of the greatest mysteries while celebrating the legacy of Amelia Earhart, a true aviation pioneer who refused to let limits define her future. Her willingness to take the first step inspired countless women to follow their own paths and pursue their dreams. It is an honor to help continue that legacy through this extraordinary mission of exploration and discovery.”

Nikumaroro is located halfway between Australia and Hawaii and lies close to 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, the planned destination of Earhart and Noonan on the third-to-last leg of their 1937 attempt to circumnavigate the world around the equator.

The expedition is being supported by Columbia Sportswear, DHL Express, Fiji Airways, Kiribati National Shipping Line, the Niswonger Foundation, Bulova and RECON Offshore, along with additional organizations providing financial, operational, logistical, technical, philanthropic, diplomatic and in-kind support, including Alvantor, Arrants Expeditions, Brownie’s Third Lung, Forestry Suppliers, GreenGood Labs, The Museum of Flight, the Naval Aviation Museum Foundation, Randolph USA, and Tricor.

  • Heidi Boraia-Tangata, Ministry of Line and Phoenix Islands Development, Kiribati representative
